chapter_text:
CHAPTER 22 - TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF SOME SPECIAL ANGLES

Introduction

In the previous chapter we defined the six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle A of a right-angled triangle: sine (sin A), cosine (cos A), tangent (tan A), cosecant (cosec A), secant (sec A) and cotangent (cot A). If in a right triangle the side opposite angle A has length p (perpendicular), the side adjacent to A has length b (base) and the hypotenuse has length h, then
   sin A = p/h,  cos A = b/h,  tan A = p/b,
   cosec A = h/p,  sec A = h/b,  cot A = b/p.
Notice the reciprocal pairs: cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A. Also tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A.

For a general angle these ratios have to be looked up in tables or found with a calculator. But for a few SPECIAL ANGLES - namely 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees - the ratios come out to exact, easily remembered values. These angles occur again and again in geometry, mensuration, heights and distances and physics, so knowing their ratios by heart is essential. This chapter derives those values from two simple triangles, assembles them into a standard table, introduces the very useful relations between the ratios of an angle and its complement, and then shows how to use all of this to evaluate expressions and to solve simple equations.

22.1 THE SPECIAL ANGLES AND WHY THEY MATTER

The special (or standard) angles are 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees. Two of them, 30 and 60, are the angles of an equilateral triangle cut in half; 45 is the acute angle of an isosceles right triangle; and 0 and 90 are the limiting cases where the acute angle of a right triangle shrinks to nothing or grows to a right angle. Because every one of these can be tied to a triangle whose sides we know exactly, the trigonometric ratios turn out to be exact surds or simple fractions rather than endless decimals.

22.2 RATIOS OF 45 DEGREES - THE ISOSCELES RIGHT TRIANGLE

Take a right-angled triangle in which the two acute angles are equal. Since the three angles add to 180 and one of them is 90, the other two must share the remaining 90 equally, so each is 45 degrees. A triangle with two equal angles is isosceles, so the two sides opposite those equal angles - the two legs - are equal. Let each leg have length 1. By the Pythagoras theorem the hypotenuse h satisfies h^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 = 2, so h = sqrt(2).

Now read off the ratios of the 45 degree angle. The perpendicular and base are both 1 and the hypotenuse is sqrt(2):
   sin 45 = perpendicular/hypotenuse = 1/sqrt(2),
   cos 45 = base/hypotenuse = 1/sqrt(2),
   tan 45 = perpendicular/base = 1/1 = 1.
The reciprocals follow at once: cosec 45 = sqrt(2), sec 45 = sqrt(2), cot 45 = 1. Note sin 45 = cos 45, which makes sense because a 45 degree angle is its own complement (90 - 45 = 45).

22.3 RATIOS OF 30 AND 60 DEGREES - THE EQUILATERAL TRIANGLE

Start with an equilateral triangle ABC in which every side has length 2 and every angle is 60 degrees. Drop a perpendicular AD from vertex A to the opposite side BC. In an equilateral triangle this perpendicular bisects both the base and the angle at A. So BD = DC = 1, and angle BAD = 30 degrees while angle ABD = 60 degrees. Triangle ABD is now a right triangle (right angle at D) with hypotenuse AB = 2 and base BD = 1. By Pythagoras the height AD = sqrt(AB^2 - BD^2) = sqrt(4 - 1) = sqrt(3).

Look at the 60 degree angle (angle ABD). Its opposite side (perpendicular) is AD = sqrt(3), its adjacent side (base) is BD = 1, and the hypotenuse is AB = 2. Hence
   sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2,  cos 60 = 1/2,  tan 60 = sqrt(3)/1 = sqrt(3).
Now look at the 30 degree angle (angle BAD) in the same triangle. Relative to this angle the opposite side is BD = 1 and the adjacent side is AD = sqrt(3), while the hypotenuse is still AB = 2. Hence
   sin 30 = 1/2,  cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2,  tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3).
The reciprocals give cosec 30 = 2, sec 30 = 2/sqrt(3), cot 30 = sqrt(3); and cosec 60 = 2/sqrt(3), sec 60 = 2, cot 60 = 1/sqrt(3). Observe how the ratios of 30 and 60 are swapped: sin 30 = cos 60, cos 30 = sin 60, tan 30 = cot 60. Again this is because 30 and 60 are complementary (30 + 60 = 90).

22.4 RATIOS OF 0 AND 90 DEGREES - THE LIMITING CASES

Imagine a right triangle whose acute angle A is made smaller and smaller. The side opposite A (the perpendicular) shrinks towards 0 while the adjacent side approaches the hypotenuse. In the limit A = 0 the perpendicular is 0 and the base equals the hypotenuse, so
   sin 0 = 0,  cos 0 = 1,  tan 0 = 0.
Their reciprocals: cot 0 and cosec 0 involve division by 0 and are NOT DEFINED, while sec 0 = 1.

Now let A grow towards 90 degrees. Then the base shrinks to 0 and the perpendicular approaches the hypotenuse, giving
   sin 90 = 1,  cos 90 = 0,  tan 90 is NOT DEFINED (division by the zero base).
Their reciprocals: cosec 90 = 1, sec 90 is NOT DEFINED, cot 90 = 0. Whenever a ratio would require dividing by zero we say it is 'not defined' (sometimes written as infinity for tan 90 and sec 90). These undefined values are just as important to remember as the numerical ones.

22.5 THE TABLE OF STANDARD VALUES

Collecting all of the above into one table (angles across the top, ratios down the side):

  Angle ->      0        30          45          60          90
  sin           0        1/2         1/sqrt(2)   sqrt(3)/2   1
  cos           1        sqrt(3)/2   1/sqrt(2)   1/2         0
  tan           0        1/sqrt(3)   1           sqrt(3)     not defined
  cosec       n.d.       2           sqrt(2)     2/sqrt(3)   1
  sec           1        2/sqrt(3)   sqrt(2)     2           not defined
  cot         n.d.       sqrt(3)     1           1/sqrt(3)   0

(Here 'n.d.' means not defined.) A handy way to remember the sine row is to write the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 under the angles 0, 30, 45, 60, 90, divide each by 4 and take the square root: sqrt(0/4)=0, sqrt(1/4)=1/2, sqrt(2/4)=1/sqrt(2), sqrt(3/4)=sqrt(3)/2, sqrt(4/4)=1. The cosine row is the same list read backwards. Once sine and cosine are known, tan = sin/cos, and the last three rows are just reciprocals. Some useful decimal approximations: 1/sqrt(2) is about 0.707, sqrt(3)/2 is about 0.866, sqrt(3) is about 1.732 and 1/sqrt(3) is about 0.577.

22.6 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS OF COMPLEMENTARY ANGLES

Two angles are COMPLEMENTARY if they add up to 90 degrees. In a right triangle the two acute angles are always complementary: if one is A the other is 90 - A. What is the perpendicular for angle A is the base for angle (90 - A), and vice versa, while the hypotenuse is shared. Swapping the roles of perpendicular and base turns each ratio into its 'co-ratio'. This gives the complementary-angle relations, valid for every acute angle A:
   sin(90 - A) = cos A,      cos(90 - A) = sin A,
   tan(90 - A) = cot A,      cot(90 - A) = tan A,
   sec(90 - A) = cosec A,    cosec(90 - A) = sec A.
The prefix 'co' in cosine, cotangent and cosecant literally records this pairing: the cosine of an angle is the sine of its COmplement. These identities let us convert the ratio of a large angle into the ratio of a smaller one. For example sin 60 = sin(90 - 30) = cos 30, and tan 80 = cot 10. They are also the quickest way to simplify expressions such as sin 18 / cos 72, because cos 72 = cos(90 - 18) = sin 18, so the quotient is 1.

22.7 EVALUATING EXPRESSIONS AT STANDARD ANGLES

To evaluate an expression, substitute the exact values from the table and simplify carefully, rationalising surds where helpful.

Example 1. Evaluate sin 30 cos 60 + cos 30 sin 60.
   = (1/2)(1/2) + (sqrt(3)/2)(sqrt(3)/2) = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1.
(In fact this equals sin(30 + 60) = sin 90 = 1.)

Example 2. Evaluate tan^2 60 + 2 tan^2 45.
   tan 60 = sqrt(3) so tan^2 60 = 3; tan 45 = 1 so tan^2 45 = 1. The value is 3 + 2(1) = 5.

Example 3. Evaluate (cos 45)/(sec 30 + cosec 30).
   cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2); sec 30 = 2/sqrt(3); cosec 30 = 2. So the denominator is 2/sqrt(3) + 2 = (2 + 2 sqrt(3))/sqrt(3). The whole expression = (1/sqrt(2)) * (sqrt(3))/(2 + 2 sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/(2 sqrt(2)(1 + sqrt(3))). Rationalising by multiplying top and bottom by (sqrt(3) - 1) gives (3 - sqrt(3))/(2 sqrt(2)(3 - 1)) = (3 - sqrt(3))/(4 sqrt(2)) = (3 sqrt(2) - sqrt(6))/8.

Example 4. Show that cos^2 30 + sin^2 30 = 1.
   (sqrt(3)/2)^2 + (1/2)^2 = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. This is a special case of the identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1.

Example 5. Using complementary angles, evaluate (sin 35 / cos 55) + (cos 35 / sin 55).
   cos 55 = cos(90 - 35) = sin 35, so the first term is 1. sin 55 = sin(90 - 35) = cos 35, so the second term is 1. The sum is 2.

22.8 SIMPLE TRIGONOMETRIC EQUATIONS

A simple trigonometric equation involving standard angles is solved by rewriting one side so that both sides are the same ratio, then comparing angles.

Example 6. Solve sin 3A = cos(A - 26), where 3A and (A - 26) are acute angles.
   Write cos(A - 26) = sin(90 - (A - 26)) = sin(116 - A). Then sin 3A = sin(116 - A) gives 3A = 116 - A, so 4A = 116 and A = 29 degrees.

Example 7. Solve tan 2A = cot(A - 18).
   cot(A - 18) = tan(90 - (A - 18)) = tan(108 - A). So 2A = 108 - A, 3A = 108, A = 36 degrees.

Example 8. Find the acute angle theta if 2 sin theta = sqrt(3).
   sin theta = sqrt(3)/2, and from the table sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, so theta = 60 degrees.

Example 9. Find theta if tan theta = 1, 0 < theta < 90.
   From the table tan 45 = 1, so theta = 45 degrees.

These techniques - substitute standard values, use complementary relations to match ratios, then equate angles - handle almost every exercise problem in this chapter.

SUMMARY

- The special angles are 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees; their trigonometric ratios are exact and worth memorising.
- 45 degree ratios come from an isosceles right triangle (legs 1, hypotenuse sqrt(2)): sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2), tan 45 = 1.
- 30 and 60 degree ratios come from an equilateral triangle bisected (giving sides 1, sqrt(3), 2): sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3); sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 60 = sqrt(3).
- Limiting cases: sin 0 = 0, cos 0 = 1, tan 0 = 0; sin 90 = 1, cos 90 = 0; tan 90, sec 90, cosec 0 and cot 0 are not defined.
- Complementary-angle relations: sin(90 - A) = cos A, cos(90 - A) = sin A, tan(90 - A) = cot A, cot(90 - A) = tan A, sec(90 - A) = cosec A, cosec(90 - A) = sec A.
- To evaluate an expression, substitute the exact table values and simplify (rationalise surds).
- To solve a simple equation, convert one ratio into the other using a complementary relation, then equate the angles.

topics.name: Standard Angles and their Ratios
topics.description: The five standard angles 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees and the six trigonometric ratios (sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec, cot) taken at each of them, including which ratios are not defined.

topics.name: Derivation from Special Triangles
topics.description: Deriving the ratios of 45 degrees from an isosceles right triangle and of 30 and 60 degrees from a bisected equilateral triangle, using the Pythagoras theorem.

topics.name: The Table of Standard Values
topics.description: The complete table of standard values, reciprocal relationships, the sqrt(n/4) memory aid for the sine row, and common decimal approximations.

topics.name: Ratios of Complementary Angles
topics.description: Complementary angles (adding to 90 degrees) and the relations sin(90-A)=cos A, tan(90-A)=cot A, sec(90-A)=cosec A and their converses.

topics.name: Evaluating Trigonometric Expressions
topics.description: Substituting exact standard-angle values into numerical expressions and simplifying, including rationalising surds and using complementary relations to simplify.

topics.name: Simple Trigonometric Equations
topics.description: Solving simple trigonometric equations involving standard angles by matching ratios (often via complementary relations) and equating the angles.

learning_outcomes.description: List the five special angles and recall the values of sin, cos and tan at each, including which ratios are not defined at 0 and 90 degrees.
Derive the trigonometric ratios of 45 degrees from an isosceles right triangle and of 30 and 60 degrees from a bisected equilateral triangle.
Reproduce the full table of standard values for all six ratios and use reciprocal relationships to fill in cosec, sec and cot.
State and explain the trigonometric ratios of complementary angles, such as sin(90-A)=cos A and tan(90-A)=cot A.
Evaluate numerical trigonometric expressions by substituting exact standard-angle values and simplifying, including rationalising surds.
Verify identities and simplify multi-term expressions at standard angles, choosing an efficient order of substitution and simplification.
Use complementary-angle relations to simplify quotients and sums of ratios of angles that add to 90 degrees.
Solve simple trigonometric equations involving standard angles by matching ratios and equating the angles.

chapter_summary.title: Trigonometric Ratios of Some Special Angles - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter gives the exact trigonometric ratios of the standard angles 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, shows how they come from simple triangles, introduces the ratios of complementary angles, and uses both to evaluate expressions and solve simple equations.

branches.label: Standard table
details: cos is the sine row reversed
tan = sin/cos; last three rows are reciprocals

sections.heading: The special angles and the reciprocal ratios
bullets: The special (standard) angles are 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees; their ratios are exact fractions or surds.
The six ratios are sin, cos, tan and their reciprocals cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, cot = 1/tan.
Also tan A = sin A / cos A and cot A = cos A / sin A, so once sine and cosine are known the rest follow.

sections.heading: Deriving 45 degrees from an isosceles right triangle
bullets: A right triangle with two equal acute angles has both equal to 45 degrees and two equal legs.
Taking each leg as 1 gives hypotenuse sqrt(1^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(2) by Pythagoras.
Hence sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2) and tan 45 = 1; the reciprocals are cosec 45 = sec 45 = sqrt(2), cot 45 = 1.

sections.heading: Deriving 30 and 60 degrees from an equilateral triangle
bullets: Bisecting an equilateral triangle of side 2 gives a right triangle with sides 1, sqrt(3) and 2.
For 60 degrees: sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 60 = sqrt(3).
For 30 degrees: sin 30 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3).
The ratios of 30 and 60 are swapped because the two angles are complementary.

sections.heading: The table and the limiting cases
bullets: tan 90, sec 90, cosec 0 and cot 0 are not defined (division by zero).
Memory aid: write 0,1,2,3,4 under the angles, divide by 4 and take the square root to get the sine row.

sections.heading: Complementary angles and their uses
bullets: Two angles are complementary when they add to 90 degrees; the two acute angles of a right triangle are complementary.
sin(90-A)=cos A, cos(90-A)=sin A, tan(90-A)=cot A, cot(90-A)=tan A, sec(90-A)=cosec A, cosec(90-A)=sec A.
These relations simplify expressions like sin 35/cos 55 (which equals 1) and solve equations such as sin 3A = cos(A-26).

key_takeaways: Memorise the exact ratios of 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees; they appear constantly in geometry and physics.
The 45 degree ratios come from an isosceles right triangle; the 30 and 60 degree ratios from a bisected equilateral triangle.
sin 30 = 1/2, cos 60 = 1/2, tan 45 = 1, sin 45 = cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2), sin 60 = cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2.
tan 90, sec 90, cosec 0 and cot 0 are not defined because they would require dividing by zero.
Complementary-angle relations turn a co-ratio of A into the plain ratio of (90 - A): sin(90-A)=cos A, tan(90-A)=cot A, etc.
Evaluate expressions by substituting exact values and rationalising surds; solve equations by matching ratios and equating angles.

glossary.definition: One of sin, cos, tan, cosec, sec or cot of an angle, defined from the sides of a right triangle.
One of 0, 30, 45, 60 or 90 degrees, whose trigonometric ratios have exact, easily-remembered values.
The side opposite the right angle in a right-angled triangle; the longest side.
The side opposite the angle under consideration in a right triangle (the 'opposite' side).
The side adjacent to the angle under consideration in a right triangle (other than the hypotenuse).
A right triangle whose two legs are equal; each acute angle is 45 degrees. Used to derive the 45 degree ratios.
A triangle with all three sides equal and all three angles 60 degrees; bisecting it gives the 30 and 60 degree ratios.
The pairs cosec = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos and cot = 1/tan.
Two angles whose measures add up to 90 degrees, such as A and 90 - A.
An identity such as sin(90-A)=cos A or tan(90-A)=cot A relating a ratio of an angle to a co-ratio of its complement.
A value that cannot be computed because it requires dividing by zero, e.g. tan 90 or cot 0.
Rewriting a surd fraction so that its denominator is free of square roots, e.g. 1/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2)/2.
An irrational root such as sqrt(2) or sqrt(3) that cannot be written exactly as a fraction.
An equation containing trigonometric ratios of an unknown angle, solved here by matching ratios and equating angles.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Trigonometric Ratios of Some Special Angles
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Use the exact values of the ratios of 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees. Show every step of your working and rationalise surds in the final answer where required.

questions.question: Write the value of each: sin 30, cos 60, tan 45, sin 90, cos 0.
questions.explanation: Direct reading of the standard-values table.

questions.question: Using an isosceles right triangle with each leg equal to 1, derive the values of sin 45, cos 45 and tan 45.
questions.answer: The two acute angles are equal, so each is 45 degrees, and the two legs are equal; take each as 1. By Pythagoras the hypotenuse = sqrt(1^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(2). Then sin 45 = perpendicular/hypotenuse = 1/sqrt(2); cos 45 = base/hypotenuse = 1/sqrt(2); tan 45 = perpendicular/base = 1/1 = 1.
questions.explanation: Legs 1 and 1 give hypotenuse sqrt(2); read off the three ratios.

questions.question: Evaluate sin 30 cos 60 + cos 30 sin 60, showing each step.
questions.answer: Substitute: sin 30 = 1/2, cos 60 = 1/2, cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. So the expression = (1/2)(1/2) + (sqrt(3)/2)(sqrt(3)/2) = 1/4 + 3/4 = 4/4 = 1. (It is sin(30+60) = sin 90 = 1.)
questions.explanation: Substitute exact values; the two products are 1/4 and 3/4 which sum to 1.

questions.question: Evaluate tan^2 60 + 2 tan^2 45.
questions.answer: tan 60 = sqrt(3) so tan^2 60 = (sqrt(3))^2 = 3. tan 45 = 1 so tan^2 45 = 1. Therefore the value = 3 + 2(1) = 5.
questions.explanation: Square the standard values then add.

questions.question: Show that cos^2 30 + sin^2 30 = 1 using exact values.
questions.answer: cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2 so cos^2 30 = 3/4. sin 30 = 1/2 so sin^2 30 = 1/4. Sum = 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. This confirms the identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 at A = 30.
questions.explanation: Square each value and add to get 1.

questions.question: Using complementary angles, evaluate (sin 35 / cos 55) + (cos 35 / sin 55).
questions.answer: cos 55 = cos(90-35) = sin 35, so sin 35 / cos 55 = 1. sin 55 = sin(90-35) = cos 35, so cos 35 / sin 55 = 1. The sum = 1 + 1 = 2.
questions.explanation: Each quotient reduces to 1 by a complementary relation.

questions.question: Evaluate (4/3) tan^2 30 + sin^2 60 - 3 cos^2 45, showing all steps.
questions.explanation: Substitute squares, take LCD 36 and combine to -11/36.

questions.question: Solve for acute A: sin 3A = cos(A - 26).
questions.answer: Write cos(A - 26) = sin(90 - (A - 26)) = sin(116 - A). Then sin 3A = sin(116 - A) gives 3A = 116 - A, so 4A = 116 and A = 29 degrees.
questions.explanation: Convert cosine to sine of the complement, then equate angles.

questions.question: Find the acute angle theta given 2 cos theta = 1. Then state cosec theta.
questions.answer: cos theta = 1/2, and cos 60 = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees. Then cosec 60 = 1/sin 60 = 1/(sqrt(3)/2) = 2/sqrt(3).

questions.question: Reproduce the standard-values table for sin, cos and tan at 0, 30, 45, 60 and 90 degrees, and state which of these are not defined.
questions.answer: sin: sin0=0, sin30=1/2, sin45=1/sqrt(2), sin60=sqrt(3)/2, sin90=1. cos: cos0=1, cos30=sqrt(3)/2, cos45=1/sqrt(2), cos60=1/2, cos90=0. tan: tan0=0, tan30=1/sqrt(3), tan45=1, tan60=sqrt(3), tan90=not defined. Among sin, cos, tan the only one not defined is tan 90 (base is zero, division by zero).
questions.explanation: Full sin/cos/tan rows; tan 90 is the only undefined entry here.

questions.question: State the six trigonometric ratios of the complementary angle (90 - A) in terms of ratios of A.
questions.answer: sin(90 - A) = cos A; cos(90 - A) = sin A; tan(90 - A) = cot A; cot(90 - A) = tan A; sec(90 - A) = cosec A; cosec(90 - A) = sec A.

Evaluate tan^2 60 + 2 tan^2 45.
questions.answer: tan 60 = sqrt(3) so tan^2 60 = 3; tan 45 = 1 so tan^2 45 = 1. Value = 3 + 2(1) = 5.

questions.question: Evaluate (5 cos^2 60 + 4 sec^2 30 - tan^2 45) / (sin^2 30 + cos^2 30).
questions.explanation: Denominator is 1 by the identity; numerator = 67/12.

questions.question: Show that sin^2 30 + cos^2 30 = 1 using exact values.
questions.explanation: Confirms sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 at 30.

questions.question: Evaluate (sin 35 / cos 55) + (cos 35 / sin 55).
questions.answer: cos 55 = cos(90-35) = sin 35, so the first term = 1. sin 55 = sin(90-35) = cos 35, so the second term = 1. Sum = 2.

questions.question: Solve for acute A: sin 3A = cos(A - 26).
questions.answer: cos(A - 26) = sin(90 - (A - 26)) = sin(116 - A). So sin 3A = sin(116 - A) gives 3A = 116 - A, hence 4A = 116 and A = 29 degrees.
questions.explanation: Convert cosine to sine of complement, then equate angles.

questions.question: Evaluate cos 45 / (sec 30 + cosec 30).
questions.answer: cos 45 = 1/sqrt(2); sec 30 = 2/sqrt(3); cosec 30 = 2. Denominator = 2/sqrt(3) + 2 = (2 + 2 sqrt(3))/sqrt(3). Expression = (1/sqrt(2)) x sqrt(3)/(2 + 2 sqrt(3)) = sqrt(3)/(2 sqrt(2)(1 + sqrt(3))). Multiply top and bottom by (sqrt(3) - 1): = (3 - sqrt(3))/(2 sqrt(2)(2)) = (3 - sqrt(3))/(4 sqrt(2)) = (3 sqrt(2) - sqrt(6))/8.
questions.explanation: Rationalise carefully to get (3 sqrt(2) - sqrt(6))/8.

questions.question: Verify that cos 60 = 1 - 2 sin^2 30.
questions.explanation: Special case of cos 2A = 1 - 2 sin^2 A.

questions.question: Simplify tan 26 x tan 64.
questions.answer: tan 64 = tan(90 - 26) = cot 26. So tan 26 x cot 26 = tan 26 x (1/tan 26) = 1.
questions.explanation: Complement turns tan 64 into cot 26; product 1.

questions.question: Solve for acute A: tan 2A = cot(A - 18).
questions.answer: cot(A - 18) = tan(90 - (A - 18)) = tan(108 - A). So 2A = 108 - A, giving 3A = 108 and A = 36 degrees.
questions.explanation: Convert cot to tan of complement, then equate angles.

questions.question: Which is greater, sin 45 or tan 30? Justify with values.
questions.answer: sin 45 = 1/sqrt(2) which is about 0.707. tan 30 = 1/sqrt(3) which is about 0.577. Since 0.707 > 0.577, sin 45 is greater.

questions.question: Evaluate tan 48 tan 23 tan 42 tan 67.
questions.answer: tan 48 = cot 42 (since 48 = 90 - 42) and tan 67 = cot 23. So the product = (tan 42 cot 42)(tan 23 cot 23) = 1 x 1 = 1.
questions.explanation: Pair each tangent with the cotangent of its complement.

questions.question: Find the acute angle theta if 2 cos theta = 1.
questions.answer: cos theta = 1/2, and cos 60 = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees.

questions.question: State which of the six ratios are not defined at 0 degrees and at 90 degrees.
questions.answer: At 0 degrees: cosec 0 and cot 0 are not defined (sin 0 = 0). At 90 degrees: sec 90 and tan 90 are not defined (cos 90 = 0).
questions.explanation: Undefined where a zero appears in the denominator.

questions.question: Evaluate sec^2 60 - tan^2 60.
questions.answer: sec 60 = 2 so sec^2 60 = 4; tan 60 = sqrt(3) so tan^2 60 = 3. Value = 4 - 3 = 1.
questions.explanation: Special case of sec^2 A - tan^2 A = 1.

questions.question: Evaluate cos 48 - sin 42.
questions.answer: sin 42 = sin(90 - 48) = cos 48. So cos 48 - sin 42 = cos 48 - cos 48 = 0.
questions.explanation: Complement makes the two terms equal.

questions.question: Solve cos theta = sin 30 for acute theta.
questions.answer: sin 30 = 1/2, so cos theta = 1/2. Since cos 60 = 1/2, theta = 60 degrees. (Equivalently sin 30 = cos 60.)

questions.question: Evaluate (sin 30 + tan 45 - cosec 60) / (sec 30 + cos 60 + cot 45).
questions.answer: Numerator = 1/2 + 1 - 2/sqrt(3) = 3/2 - 2/sqrt(3). Denominator = 2/sqrt(3) + 1/2 + 1 = 3/2 + 2/sqrt(3). Writing 2/sqrt(3) = 2 sqrt(3)/3 and multiplying numerator and denominator by 6: numerator = 9 - 4 sqrt(3), denominator = 9 + 4 sqrt(3). Value = (9 - 4 sqrt(3))/(9 + 4 sqrt(3)). Rationalise by (9 - 4 sqrt(3)): = (9 - 4 sqrt(3))^2 / (81 - 48) = (129 - 72 sqrt(3))/33 = (43 - 24 sqrt(3))/11.

questions.question: Explain why sin 45 = cos 45 using the isosceles right triangle.
questions.answer: In an isosceles right triangle the two legs are equal, so for the 45 degree angle the opposite side equals the adjacent side (both 1) while the hypotenuse is sqrt(2). Then sin 45 = opposite/hyp = 1/sqrt(2) and cos 45 = adjacent/hyp = 1/sqrt(2), so they are equal.

questions.question: Express sin 67 + cos 75 using ratios of angles less than 45 degrees.
questions.answer: sin 67 = sin(90 - 23) = cos 23. cos 75 = cos(90 - 15) = sin 15. So sin 67 + cos 75 = cos 23 + sin 15.
questions.explanation: Rewrite each with its complement below 45.

questions.question: If sin(A + B) = 1 and cos(A - B) = sqrt(3)/2, with A and B acute, find A and B.
questions.answer: sin(A + B) = 1 means A + B = 90. cos(A - B) = sqrt(3)/2 means A - B = 30. Adding: 2A = 120 so A = 60; then B = 90 - 60 = 30. So A = 60 degrees and B = 30 degrees.
questions.explanation: Solve the two linear equations in A and B.

questions.question: An equilateral triangle ABC has each side 2 units. An altitude AD is drawn from A to BC, meeting BC at D. Using this figure answer: (a) What is the length BD? (b) What is the length of the altitude AD? (c) Find sin 60 using triangle ABD. (d) Find cos 60 using triangle ABD.
questions.answer: (a) The altitude of an equilateral triangle bisects the base, so BD = 2/2 = 1. (b) In right triangle ABD, AD = sqrt(AB^2 - BD^2) = sqrt(2^2 - 1^2) = sqrt(4 - 1) = sqrt(3). (c) For the 60 degree angle ABD, opposite = AD = sqrt(3), hypotenuse = AB = 2, so sin 60 = sqrt(3)/2. (d) adjacent = BD = 1, hypotenuse = 2, so cos 60 = 1/2.
questions.explanation: Bisected equilateral triangle gives sides 1, sqrt(3), 2.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, and its two legs PQ and QR are each 5 units, so the acute angles at P and R are each 45 degrees. Answer: (a) Find the hypotenuse PR. (b) Find sin 45. (c) Find tan 45.
questions.answer: (a) By Pythagoras PR = sqrt(PQ^2 + QR^2) = sqrt(25 + 25) = sqrt(50) = 5 sqrt(2). (b) For a 45 degree angle, sin 45 = opposite/hypotenuse = 5/(5 sqrt(2)) = 1/sqrt(2). (c) tan 45 = opposite/adjacent = 5/5 = 1.
questions.explanation: Equal legs 5 give hypotenuse 5 sqrt(2); ratios independent of leg length.

questions.question: A student is asked to evaluate three expressions using the standard-value table. Evaluate: (a) sin 30 + cos 60; (b) tan 45 - cot 45; (c) 2 sin 60 cos 60.
questions.answer: (a) sin 30 + cos 60 = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. (b) tan 45 - cot 45 = 1 - 1 = 0. (c) 2 sin 60 cos 60 = 2 (sqrt(3)/2)(1/2) = 2 (sqrt(3)/4) = sqrt(3)/2. (Note this equals sin 120, but as a value it is sqrt(3)/2.)
questions.explanation: Substitute exact values and simplify each part.

questions.question: In many problems the two angles involved add up to 90 degrees, so complementary-angle relations simplify the work. Using them, evaluate: (a) sin 40 / cos 50; (b) tan 25 tan 65; (c) sin^2 30 + sin^2 60.
questions.answer: (a) cos 50 = cos(90 - 40) = sin 40, so sin 40 / cos 50 = 1. (b) tan 65 = tan(90 - 25) = cot 25, so tan 25 tan 65 = tan 25 cot 25 = 1. (c) sin 60 = cos 30, but more directly sin^2 30 + sin^2 60 = (1/2)^2 + (sqrt(3)/2)^2 = 1/4 + 3/4 = 1.
questions.explanation: Each part reduces using a complement to 90 degrees.

questions.question: A worksheet asks students to find the acute angle theta in each simple equation. Solve: (a) sin theta = 1/2; (b) cos theta = 1/2; (c) tan theta = 1; (d) sin theta = 1.
questions.answer: (a) sin 30 = 1/2, so theta = 30 degrees. (b) cos 60 = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees. (c) tan 45 = 1, so theta = 45 degrees. (d) sin 90 = 1, so theta = 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: Match each ratio value to the standard table.

questions.question: Evaluate each of the following using the standard values: (a) sin^2 30 + cos^2 45; (b) (4/3) tan^2 30; (c) cos^2 60.
questions.explanation: Square the standard values then combine.

questions.question: A table of reciprocal ratios is being completed. Using the standard values, fill in: (a) cosec 45; (b) sec 45; (c) cosec 60; (d) cot 30.
questions.answer: (a) cosec 45 = 1/sin 45 = sqrt(2). (b) sec 45 = 1/cos 45 = sqrt(2). (c) cosec 60 = 1/sin 60 = 2/sqrt(3). (d) cot 30 = 1/tan 30 = sqrt(3).
questions.explanation: Each is the reciprocal of the corresponding sin, cos or tan.

questions.question: Two acute angles of a right triangle are A and 90 - A, so they are complementary. Using complementary relations, rewrite each in terms of a ratio of A: (a) cos(90 - A); (b) cot(90 - A); (c) cosec(90 - A).
questions.answer: (a) cos(90 - A) = sin A. (b) cot(90 - A) = tan A. (c) cosec(90 - A) = sec A.
questions.explanation: Each co-ratio of the complement becomes the plain ratio of A.

questions.question: The identity sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1 should hold at every angle. Check it at the standard angles: (a) verify it at A = 45; (b) verify it at A = 60; (c) state the value at A = 0.
questions.explanation: The identity gives 1 at every angle checked.

questions.question: Read the standard table at the limiting angles. State: (a) sin 0 and cos 0; (b) sin 90 and cos 90; (c) tan 0 and tan 90 (say if undefined).
questions.answer: (a) sin 0 = 0 and cos 0 = 1. (b) sin 90 = 1 and cos 90 = 0. (c) tan 0 = 0, and tan 90 is not defined (because cos 90 = 0 makes sin90/cos90 a division by zero).
